title: Why Rust: ownership, borrowing and the mental model
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Rust suits tools that must be fast, small and safe: command line utilities, agents that run on every host, proxies, parsers and controllers.
Every value has one owner, and the value is dropped when the owner goes out of scope.
You can lend a value with a reference.
A reference must not outlive the value it points to.
Rust errors are detailed and often suggest the fix.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The value used after it moved
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A first Rust tool failed to compile after a variable was passed to a function and used again.
An operator runs a command such as: cargo build 2>&1 | head -6
The function took ownership of config, so it could not be used afterwards.
Passing a reference instead, `run(&config)`, kept the owner in main.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Cloning everything to silence the compiler.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Errors: Option, Result and the question mark
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: `Option<T>` is either `Some(value)` or `None`.
`Result<T, E>` is either `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`.
Inside a function that returns a Result, `?` after an expression returns early with the error if there was one, and otherwise gives the Ok value.
For libraries, define an error enum with the `thiserror` crate, so callers can match on the cause.
A panic stops the thread and is for bugs, such as an impossible state.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A panic at three in the morning
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A cleanup tool crashed on an unexpected file name and left a job half done.
An operator runs a command such as: ./cleanup --dir /data/tmp
The code used unwrap on a file operation.
It was changed to return a Result with context that names the path, the tool now reports the error and continues with the next file, and the exit code distinguishes partial failure from success.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: unwrap on user input and files.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Structs, enums, traits and generics
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A struct groups named fields. This keeps the next step safe and easy to check.
Each variant of an enum may carry data.
A trait defines methods a type can implement, like an interface.
Generic functions work for many types: `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(items: &[T])`.
`#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]` generates common implementations.

title: Failure and recovery: A state that should not exist
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A deploy tool reported a running service with no process id, because states were booleans and strings.
An operator runs a command such as: grep -n "is_running" src/*.rs | head -3
The struct allowed is_running true with pid None, and unwrap panicked.
Replacing both fields with an enum whose Running variant carries the pid made that state impossible, and the compiler pointed to every place that needed an update.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Booleans and strings instead of enums.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: CLI tools with clap, serde and files
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: `cargo new tool` creates a binary crate.
With the derive feature, a struct describes the command line and clap generates parsing, help text and error messages.
Define a struct for the configuration and derive Deserialize.
Print results to standard output and diagnostics to standard error, so pipes work.
Unit test the library functions with ordinary tests.

title: Failure and recovery: A tool that always exited zero
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A CI check built in Rust passed every build because it exited with zero on errors.
An operator runs a command such as: ./check-config bad.yaml; echo "exit=$?"
The main function printed the error and returned normally.
Changing it to return a Result from main made the process exit with a non zero code.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Printing errors but exiting zero.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Async Rust with Tokio and network services
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: An `async fn` returns a future, a value that does nothing until it is awaited.
Tokio provides a runtime that schedules tasks over a pool of threads.
Wrap remote calls in `tokio::time::timeout`, because a network call without one can wait forever.
Tasks communicate through channels such as `mpsc`, which avoids sharing memory.
A blocking call such as a heavy computation or a synchronous file read stops a worker thread and starves other tasks.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A service that froze under load
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
An exporter stopped answering health checks when one handler read a large file.
An operator runs a command such as: curl -s -m 2 localhost:9100/health; echo "exit=$?"
The handler used a blocking file read on the runtime thread, so with a few slow reads all workers were busy and health checks timed out.
Using tokio::fs and spawn_blocking for the heavy parse restored responsiveness.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Blocking calls on the runtime.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Testing, cross compilation and shipping static binaries
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Unit tests live next to the code in a `#[cfg(test)]` module and integration tests in the `tests` directory.
Run `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` and `cargo test` on every change.
Add a target with `rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` and build with `--target`.
Set `opt-level`, `lto = true`, `codegen-units = 1` and `strip = true` in the release profile to shrink and speed up the binary at the cost of build time.
Copy the static binary into a scratch or distroless image for a very small container with little to attack.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A binary that would not start on the server
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A tool built on a developer laptop failed on an older server with a missing library version.
An operator runs a command such as: ./agent --version
The binary was linked dynamically against a newer libc than the server had.
Building for the musl target in CI produced a static binary that ran everywhere, and the pipeline now tests the artifact in a container with an old distribution.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Building releases on laptops.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
